text: Then Bildad the Shuhite answered:
How long will you go on hunting for words? Think it through, and then we can talk.

versions.text: How long before you put an end to words? Come to your senses, and then we can talk.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew קִנְצֵי is difficult; the sense is likely "how long will you set snares/limits with words." "Come to your senses" for תָּבִינוּ ("understand, consider") is more paraphrastic than the Hebrew warrants.

text: Why are we counted as cattle, reckoned unclean in your eyes?

versions.text: Why are we counted as cattle, considered stupid in your eyes?
versions.explanation: נִטְמִינוּ derives from טמא/טמה, meaning "deemed unclean/stupid." "Stupid" is a defensible reading, but "unclean" better parallels the animal imagery and keeps a more literal sense; consider a footnote noting the alternative.

text: You who tear yourself to pieces in your anger — shall the earth be abandoned for your sake, or the rock be moved from its place?
Indeed, the light of the wicked is extinguished; the flame of his fire no longer shines.

versions.text: Yes, the light of the wicked goes out; the flame of his fire gives no light.
versions.explanation: "Yes" at the start is weak for oral reading; "Indeed" or "Surely" carries גַּם better. "Gives no light" is acceptable but "no longer shines" reads more smoothly aloud.

versions.text: Indeed, the lamp of the wicked goes out; the flame of his fire no longer shines.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew here is אוֹר ("light"), while נֵר ("lamp") appears only in the next verse. Rendering אוֹר as "lamp" blurs the deliberate progression from "light" (v. 5) to "his lamp" (v. 6) and duplicates the imagery unnecessarily. The revision retains the improved rhythm of the second line while restoring the correct noun.

text: The light in his tent grows dark, and the lamp above him is snuffed out.
His vigorous stride is cut short, and his own schemes throw him down.
By his own feet he is thrust into a net; he walks straight into the mesh.

versions.text: For his own feet drive him into a net; he wanders onto its mesh.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew is passive (שֻׁלַּח, "he is sent/thrust") with בְּרַגְלָיו, "by his feet." Also "onto its mesh" — the mesh/netting is a separate snare, not the net's own mesh; "into the mesh" avoids the false possessive.

versions.text: His feet carry him into a net; he wanders into its mesh.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew verb שֻׁלַּח is passive ("he is sent/thrust"), with בְּרַגְלָיו indicating the means ("by his feet"); "his feet carry him" turns it into an active clause and loses the sense of the man being caught by an outside power. Also, the שְׂבָכָה is a separate snare, not the netting belonging to the previously mentioned net, so the possessive "its mesh" should be avoided.

text: A trap seizes him by the heel; a snare holds him fast.
A rope lies hidden for him in the ground, a snare across his path.
Terrors startle him on every side and chase him at his heels.
Hunger wastes away his strength; ruin waits ready for his fall.

versions.text: His strength is famished; disaster stands ready at his side.
versions.explanation: "His strength is famished" is awkward in English. Also לְצַלְעוֹ can mean "for his stumbling/fall" as well as "at his side"; "for his fall" fits the parallel of impending calamity.

text: Disease eats away his skin; the firstborn of death devours his limbs.

versions.text: It devours patches of his skin; the firstborn of death consumes his limbs.
versions.explanation: "It devours" has no clear antecedent for oral hearers, since the subject only appears in the second line. Naming the agent (or restructuring so "the firstborn of death" governs both lines) makes the verse clear when read aloud.

text: He is torn from the safety of his tent and marched off to the king of terrors.
Strangers settle in his tent, for nothing of his remains; burning sulfur is scattered over his dwelling.

versions.text: Fire settles in his tent, where nothing of his remains; burning sulfur is scattered over his dwelling.
versions.explanation: The subject of the feminine verb תִּשְׁכּוֹן is unstated; "fire" is a conjecture. Since the verse itself introduces sulfur only in the second line, an alternative rendering ("nothing of his dwells there" or "others dwell") is preferable, or add a footnote noting the Hebrew is uncertain.

text: Below, his roots dry up; above, his branches wither.
His memory perishes from the earth; he has no name in the streets.
He is driven from light into darkness and banished from the world.
He leaves no offspring or descendant among his people, no survivor where he once lived.
Those who come after are appalled at his fate; those who went before are seized with horror.

versions.text: Those in the west are appalled at his fate; those in the east are seized with horror.
versions.explanation: אַחֲרֹנִים/קַדְמֹנִים most naturally mean "later ones/earlier ones" (generations) in this context; the geographical rendering "west/east" is a secondary sense and obscures the temporal contrast, which fits the theme of his memory perishing (v. 17). A footnote could note the alternative "in the west... in the east."

text: Surely such are the dwellings of the wicked, and this is the place of the one who does not know God.

versions.text: Surely such is the dwelling of the unjust, the place of one who does not know God.
versions.explanation: מִשְׁכְּנוֹת is plural, and the second line begins with וְזֶה, "and this is," which the current rendering drops, flattening the two-part structure of the closing line.
